entry.title: Peakd Blog, a blog that is truly yours

link.title: Peakd Blog, a blog that is truly yours

entry.content:
A while back, I shared [a sneak peek at a project I was working on](https://peakd.com/hive-139531/@asgarth/a-sneak-peek-at-a-new-project-coming-soon). There were screenshots, quite a few themes, and a conveniently vague “coming soon.” Well, it finally has a link I can share. PeakD Blog is live at **[peakd.blog](https://peakd.blog).** The idea is simple: give your Hive writing a home that feels like your own website. Your posts, your profile, your style, and an address you can put on a business card, share with a friend, or add to your social profiles. ## Your writing, with a place of its own If you already publish on PeakD, you already have the content to get started. ![image.png](https://files.peakd.com/file/peakd-hive/asgarth/23u6Yr2NYjaoznaioWdQMDMBKEid8Z1114ivw9qsS4q2zVpXKsEb2wJjnqX328ziuL6T4.png) PeakD Blog brings your existing Hive posts together in a dedicated blog, with an archive, individual article pages, and About and Contact pages based on your Hive profile. You keep publishing through PeakD, and your posts appear on your blog. The content stays on Hive, and your blog settings are saved in your account metadata. Once you've claimed your blog, anyone can open it and read your articles without signing in or having a Hive account. That makes it an easy link to share with people who are interested in your writing and might be discovering Hive for the first time. PeakD remains the place to write, discover communities, and take part in the wider Hive experience. Your blog gives people a place to spend time with your work. ## Pick a look that feels like you If you read the preview, you might remember that I got a little carried away with the themes. That hasn't really changed. There are clean personal blogs, photography-focused designs, bold typography, field notebooks, retro pixels, and terminal-inspired layouts. The themes have their own character, including how they handle navigation, archives, and article pages. **Default, Minimalist, Brutalist, and Aperture are available to everyone**, with more designs choices available through [PeakD Horizon](https://peakd.com/@peakd/subscriptions). Depending on the theme, you can choose top or side navigation, list or grid views, content width, light or dark mode, and accent colors. You can also change your blog's name and description, preview your choices, and save them through your wallet. I wanted this part to be fun: try a few things, find something you like, and get back to writing. ## A few useful details Alongside the design choices, there are some practical features to help people enjoy and follow your work: - **Topic browsing:** enable a topic bar so readers can find more posts about the subjects they like. - **RSS:** readers can follow your blog in their preferred feed reader. - **Sharing:** article pages include sharing options and previews for links shared elsewhere. - **Mobile layouts:** your blog adapts to phones, tablets, and larger screens. - **Interface languages:** optional localization lets readers use the navigation and interface in their preferred supported language. Your articles stay in the language you wrote them in. And the Hive connection is still there. Readers with a Hive account can connect a supported wallet, choose their vote weight, comment, and reply directly on the blog. Those interactions happen on Hive, with signing handled by the wallet. ## A little more room with Horizon You can get started for free. The free blog shows posts published through PeakD and includes the four free themes mentioned above. An active **[PeakD Horizon subscription](https://peakd.com/@peakd/subscriptions) for the blog owner** adds: - **Posts from other Hive publishing apps**, so your blog can bring together writing published across Hive. - **Premium themes**, for more ways to make the site your own. - **Up to three posts pinned in your navigation**, useful for a “Start here” guide, a project introduction, or information you want visitors to find easily. - **A portfolio gallery**, displaying images from posts you've marked “Show in Portfolio” on PeakD, with topic filters and a full-screen image viewer. If you already have Horizon on the account that owns your blog, those extras are available to that blog. Readers don't need Horizon to visit it. ## More than a place for the latest post This is the part I'm looking forward to seeing people use. A travel writer could turn years of posts into a journal worth exploring. A photographer or artist could pair their stories with a portfolio. Someone building a project could pin an introduction and keep publishing updates under one address. There is also a **Products page for accounts with their Hive shop enabled**, bringing existing product and subscription listings into the blog. That gives people another way to discover what you offer alongside your writing. You may already have a lot of useful work on Hive. A dedicated blog gives you another way to put it in front of people, including people outside our usual circles. ## Give it a try Getting started is straightforward: 1. Visit **[peakd.blog](https://peakd.blog)** and enter your Hive username. 2. Connect the wallet for that account to open your owner preview. 3. Open **Customize blog**, try the available settings, and preview the result. 4. Choose **Claim & Save** and approve the operation in your wallet. 5. Share **`yourname.peakd.blog`** and keep publishing through PeakD. Until you claim it, the blog preview is only accessible to you as the owner. Claiming makes the blog public; your existing Hive posts remain public on Hive throughout. If you're new to Hive, you can [create an account](https://signup.hive.io/) first and start from there. I'm happy to finally get this into people's hands. If you set up a blog, drop your link in the comments — I'd love to see which themes you choose and what you do with it. Feedback, suggestions, and the inevitable “this looks a bit strange on my phone” reports are welcome here or [on Discord](https://discord.gg/uPxmXjX). **[Come have a look at peakd.blog](https://peakd.blog).**
Source: Peakd Blog, a blog that is truly yours by @asgarth

entry.title: Ecency Web 4.4.3 - Faster, More Social, More Fun

link.title: Ecency Web 4.4.3 - Faster, More Social, More Fun

entry.content:
A new Ecency release is here! 🚀 Version **4.4.3** brings a large collection of improvements across Ecency - from faster feeds and better reading performance to major upgrades for curation, chat, audio, and the first steps into something a little more playful. A lot has changed under the hood too. This release includes dozens of fixes and optimizations aimed at making Ecency faster, more reliable, and more resilient across desktop and mobile. Here are some of the highlights. Faster feeds and reading ------------------------ Speed has been a major focus of this release. Feeds, community pages, profiles, and individual posts have received significant rendering and caching improvements. More content can now arrive with the initial page response, helping pages become useful sooner instead of waiting for additional client-side loading. Feed navigation has also been improved to make returning to content feel more natural. Cached rows can be restored during navigation, feed cards now have unique identifiers for restoring reading position, unnecessary image/GIF requests have been reduced, and several sources of perceived slowness have been removed. The result: **less waiting and a smoother experience while browsing Ecency.** Curation Desk gets much more powerful ------------------------------------- The **Curation Desk** continues to evolve into a serious workspace for community curation. This release adds and improves: * A curator roster administration panel * Quick actions for recommended posts * Better mobile support for reviewing and marking posts * Smarter handling of already-reviewed recommendations * More accurate recommendation counts * Improved review workflow and toolbar * Guest curator applications, which is open at the moment, go Apply: [https://ecency.com/curation/applications](https://ecency.com/curation/applications) * Tools for curation teams to review and elect guest curators * Better handling and labeling of excluded content These changes make it easier for curation teams to organize themselves, discover content, and collaborate on rewarding valuable contributions. Better group chats and private channels --------------------------------------- Ecency Chat also received a substantial update. Group conversations are now supported on the web, along with improvements such as seeing who reacted to messages, displaying sender names correctly in groups, renaming groups, sorting conversations by activity, and showing previews for post links. The New Chat experience and responsive layouts have been polished as well, making conversations easier to manage across different screen sizes. Listen with natural voices -------------------------- Reading isn't always the most convenient way to enjoy a great Hive post. The new **Listen** experience introduces natural-voice audio generation for posts, unlocked using Ecency Points. Instead of relying on the browser's Web Speech text-to-speech system, Ecency can generate a more natural listening experience. The player includes playback speeds up to **2.5×** and shows generation progress while your audio is being prepared. Whether you're walking, driving, exercising, or simply prefer listening, this gives you another way to experience content on Hive. Welcome to Raidstead -------------------- Something different has also been growing inside Ecency. **Raidstead** is a new community raid game where alliances become towns, players rally together, build their war chest and town, follow their allies' progress, and prepare to face weekly pests. The first version introduces the Raidstead world, heroes, alliance towns, a pre-season field guide, weekly pest reveals, progress tracking, town news, season countdowns, and more. HiveSigner users can participate too. This is an experiment in making community participation more interactive and fun - and we're looking forward to seeing where it goes. Reliability, security and SDK improvements ------------------------------------------ A lot of work in 4.4.3 isn't immediately visible, but it matters just as much. We've strengthened several areas of the application, including safer handling of untrusted metadata, improved error handling, protection against malformed content, URL-secret redaction from error reports, safer opening of external tabs, and better handling of taken-down content. The Ecency SDK also received important transaction improvements, including transaction-size validation, better compatibility with encrypted memos, node failover when broadcasting transactions, improved block references for lagging nodes, correct authority serialization, and safer retries for ambiguous AI Assist requests. Image uploads now retry temporary server failures as well, alongside numerous fixes for media rendering, metadata, editors, feeds, profiles, Waves, and browser-specific issues. Are you developer and building your own app on Hive? Go try out `@ecency/sdk` library smart and convenient... Better media everywhere ----------------------- This release includes a number of smaller changes that add up to a better media experience. YouTube Shorts now render in their proper vertical format, 3Speak audio embeds appear as audio players rather than video frames, GIF handling has been improved, list thumbnails maintain their intended 16:9 ratio, classic editor previews can display video embeds, and NSFW media in Waves is covered appropriately. We've also improved compatibility with content originating from other Hive applications. Community contributions ----------------------- Open source remains an important part of Ecency. A warm welcome to **@hiveuprss** and **@tibfox**, who made their first contributions to Ecency Vision in this release. ❤️ And, as always, thank you to everyone reporting bugs, testing changes, suggesting improvements, curating content, building communities, and simply using Ecency every day. What's next? ------------ Ecency continues to grow beyond being simply another interface for Hive. We're improving the fundamentals - **speed, reliability, publishing, reading and discovery** - while also building better tools for **communities, curation, communication and new ways to interact with content**. Version 4.4.3 is a big step in that direction. Update, explore the new features, try the Curation Desk, start a group conversation, listen to a post - and maybe pay Raidstead a visit while you're there. ⚔️ See you around Ecency! 💙

entry.title: HafSQL v2.7.0
entry.content:
# HafSQL v2.7.0: changes for public database users ## Removed tables - **`hafsql.rc_delegations_table`** is gone. Use the `hafsql.rc_delegations` view, which now reads from balance_tracker. - **`hafsql.proposal_approvals_table`** is gone. Use the `hafsql.proposal_approvals` view, which now reads from hafbe. ## Removed columns from `hafsql.accounts_table` `reward_hive_balance`, `reward_hbd_balance`, `reward_vests_balance`, `to_withdraw`, `vesting_withdraw_rate`, `withdrawn` and `proxy` are gone. The `hafsql.accounts` **view** still has all of them under the same names. They now come from balance_tracker / hafbe. If you queried `accounts_table` directly, switch to the view. ## View columns that changed (same names, different values or types) | View.column | Before | Now | |---|---|---| | `delegations.vests` | raw ×1,000,000 | VESTS, `numeric(27,6)` | | `accounts.incoming_vests` / `outgoing_vests` | raw ×1,000,000 | VESTS. `*_hp` columns unchanged | | `accounts.to_withdraw` | remaining amount, dropped after each payout | total power-down amount (as in hived) | | `accounts.vesting_withdraw_rate` | to_withdraw / 13 | rounded up, as hived does since HF21 | | `accounts.next_vesting_withdrawal` | drifted 3s per weekly payout | exact. `NULL` when no power down is active | | `rc_delegations.rc` | `text` | numeric | | `rc_delegations.timestamp` | last sync time of the row | block time of the delegation op | | `comments.net_rshares` | sum of absolute rshares | signed sum (downvotes subtract) | | `comments.abs_rshares` | n/a | **new column**: sum of absolute rshares | | `comments.total_rshares` / `net_rshares` | changed votes counted twice | only each voter's latest vote counts | | `operation_account_update*_table.json_metadata` / `posting_json_metadata` | `{}` when the op left it empty | `NULL` (empty means "unchanged" on chain) | ## Behavior changes - **Comments deleted and then re-posted** at the same permlink are now a new row with a **new `id`**, the same as hivemind. Before, they stayed marked as deleted. - **Weekly market buckets** now run Monday to Sunday. Before, Sunday trades landed in the next week. Existing buckets are rebuilt. - **`hafsql.get_timestamp`, `hafsql.id_from_timestamp` and `comments.cashout_time` / `last_payout`** now give correct results when your session timezone isn't UTC. - **`hafsql.get_timestamp`** now also accepts a block number (`int4`). - **`hafd.operation_id_to_type_id`** was removed from the docs. ## Fixes (no query changes needed) - Reblog permlinks were wrong. - Account metadata was wiped by updates with empty metadata. - Comment titles were blanked by edits with an empty title. - `get_balance(account, block)` and `balances_history` were slow.

entry.title: PR #141: Letting Hive-Engine Lite Nodes Catch Up Before Cleaning House

link.title: PR #141: Letting Hive-Engine Lite Nodes Catch Up Before Cleaning House

entry.content:
Hey everyone, In my last update, I broke down the Knobs A, B, and C changes and teased what was coming next. The latest piece of that puzzle, **Knobs D**, is now built, tested on live mainnet traffic, and submitted as [PR #141](https://github.com/hive-engine/hivesmartcontracts/pull/141) against the `qa` branch. This round focuses squarely on lite-node operations: specifically, teaching the node to hold off on pruning local database history when it has more urgent work to do. ## The Problem: Housekeeping During a Fire Lite nodes stay small and efficient by periodically running cleanup jobs (`database.cleanupLightNode()`) to purge old blocks and transactions they no longer need. Under normal conditions, this background housekeeping runs quietly and everyone is happy. The trouble starts when a node falls behind. Whether it's scheduled server maintenance, an unexpected reboot, or an upstream network hiccup, a node that wakes up thousands of blocks behind the chain head needs all the CPU cycles and disk I/O it can get just to ingest and validate incoming blocks. Having MongoDB stop what it's doing every few minutes to execute heavy delete operations right in the middle of a catch-up sprint is the database equivalent of vacuuming the living room while the house is on fire. It causes unnecessary I/O contention and drags out the time it takes to get back to the head block. The fix is straightforward in concept: make cleanup lag-aware. If the node is struggling to catch up, let it defer cleanup for a bit and focus on block ingestion. Crucially, this doesn't touch block processing order, smart contracts, or consensus rules. It strictly changes _when_ local pruning takes place. ## The New Configuration Knobs The adaptive cleanup behavior is completely opt-in and controlled under the `lightNode` configuration block: ```json { "lightNode": { "enabled": true, "adaptiveCleanup": true, "cleanupLagThreshold": 1000, "maxConsecutiveCleanupSkips": 3, "lastVerifiedBlockCacheTTL": 900000 } } ``` Here’s how these pieces work together: - **`adaptiveCleanup`**: Enables the lag-aware logic. If left `false` (the default), the node behaves exactly as it always has. - **`cleanupLagThreshold`**: How many blocks behind the node needs to be before it starts skipping cleanup passes. In this example, if the node is more than 1,000 blocks behind head, it postpones pruning. - **`maxConsecutiveCleanupSkips`**: The safety valve. We can't let a node defer cleanup indefinitely while syncing a massive backlog, or local disk usage would balloon. Setting this to `3` means the node will skip at most three consecutive cleanup cycles before forcing a cleanup pass anyway, regardless of lag. - **`lastVerifiedBlockCacheTTL`**: Caches the lookup for `lastVerifiedBlockNumber` in memory for 15 minutes (900,000 ms). That last setting is a quiet efficiency win. Previously, every single cleanup pass did a full database lookup against `witnesses.params` to find the last verified block height. Since round verification only advances every ~40 minutes (~1,200 blocks), re-querying the database every cleanup cycle was pure waste. Because verified block height only moves forward, a cached value is inherently safe: the absolute worst case is that the node retains an extra 15 minutes of old blocks before pruning them. It can never cause the node to delete data too aggressively. ## Live Testing on a 19,000-Block Catch-Up Unit tests are good for checking logic, but I always prefer seeing how these changes behave under actual pressure. I've been running this branch on my live witness setup since October 5th. As luck would have it, my test node ended up falling about **19,000 blocks behind**: giving me a far more realistic stress test than any tidy benchmark I could have staged. Watching `journalctl` during the catch-up confirmed the safety limits were working exactly as designed. The node fell into a predictable rhythm: three skipped cleanup passes followed by one forced cleanup pass, repeating continuously while it processed the backlog. ![screenshot-20261017-092502.png](https://files.peakd.com/file/peakd-hive/thecrazygm/23tRtNZZJsvSoXvQgfUVR9YFxNKHz43w9G1WokygUnnPfGsWpSdKyDBTAY9Hu2HsGVrwt.png) Over the course of the run, the logs recorded **90 skipped cleanups and 30 forced cleanups**. The lag steadily dropped from 19,000 blocks down past the 1,000-block threshold, at which point normal periodic cleanup resumed smoothly. The node is now sitting happily locked to the Hive head. ## Designing for Failure: The Fallback Guardrail One detail I was very deliberate about: what happens if the streamer encounters an RPC blip and can't accurately report chain lag? A naive implementation might assume zero lag and clean up constantly, or worse, assume infinite lag and stop cleaning up forever. Instead, if the streamer can't determine current lag, the node logs a clear warning and proceeds with the cleanup pass anyway. It’s always safer to fall back to the established default behavior when an input is uncertain. A kind of defensive edge-case handling that prevents an optimization from turning into a late-night operational headache. ## Status and Verification All of this work is wrapped up in **[PR #141](https://github.com/hive-engine/hivesmartcontracts/pull/141)**, open against the `qa` branch of `hive-engine/hivesmartcontracts`. The PR includes full configuration docs alongside focused database unit tests covering both the cleanup skip decision tree and the cached verified-block lookup (all tests passing cleanly). No complicated magic here: just giving the database a breather when it has higher-priority work on its plate, backed by firm guardrails so the garbage still gets taken out. Give it a look on `qa`, and let me know your thoughts! As always, **Michael Garcia a.k.a. TheCrazyGM**
